semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: Model provenance ≠ instance provenance. PDTF's dct:source chain from every ontology term back to the JSON Schema leaf it was minted from is genuine, verifiable provenance — of the model . Claiming it satisfies Chapter 4's instance-data lineage ask would be a material overclaim that would not survive scrutiny by anyone who reads the ontology. (The good news, established while writing this register: PDTF does have real instance-level claim provenance — prov:wasDerivedFrom is SHACL-mandatory on every opda:Claim . The strength is real; just don't cite the wrong evidence for it.)

What the standard must supply is the evidence the rule operates on : who issued a signal, when, at what assurance level, and whether a status check was performed at the point of reliance. Encode the evidence, not the verdict.

semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: Chapter 2 asks for a provenance schema carrying "issuer, inputs, timestamps, assurance level , revocation checks"; Chapter 1's CBOM needs an assurance type per credential. Do not re-add it by reflex — it was removed for a good reason (no schema basis), and re-adding it to satisfy DBT would repeat the original mistake. The right move is to ask whether an evidential-provenance scale (how authoritative is this fact about this house?) is warranted on its own merits, distinct from GPG 44/45 identity assurance. If it is, PDTF's mandatory claim provenance is the natural substrate — and no other sector in the Guidebook has one .

semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: "Schemes should rely on DVS certification, not accredit identity providers themselves" cuts against PDTF's KYC/KYB issuer onboarding. The reconciliation: PDTF's issuers are not identity providers, they are issuers of facts about properties — and DVS has no certification route for "issuer of a fact about a building". Nobody certifies HM Land Registry as an ASP. Say this plainly and early, or risk being told the accreditation function is redundant when it demonstrably is not.

semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: Chapter 3 requires that, for any datum in a property transaction, a machine can answer: who consented to this being here, under what authority, for what purpose, until when, has that been withdrawn, what obligations survive the withdrawal, who is accountable for the datum's accuracy, and who has relied on the identity check behind it — and PDTF today can answer roughly one of those nine.

semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: Ontology and Schema are two independent accounts of the same PDTF data — one in OWL/RDF, one in JSON Schema. semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: The technical semantic-modelling workstream. PDTF today is JSON Schema; the work is to elevate it to a full linked-data stack — bounded contexts → controlled vocabulary → SKOS taxonomy → OWL ontology → SHACL validation → JSON-LD mappings — so that property data is verifiably interoperable across the UK industry.
semanticReframeBlocks.replacementText: These are the PDTF 1.0-era semantic-modelling records. They explored how the published JSON Schema implementation could inform a linked-data stack — bounded contexts → controlled vocabulary → SKOS taxonomy → OWL ontology → SHACL validation → JSON-LD mappings — and now serve as qualified inputs to SPDTF 2.0 Development. Their artefacts retain their own maturity and do not inherit the schema implementation's published status.

semanticReframeBlocks.sourceText: The published, generated reference of the OPDA PDTF ontology itself — the canonical specification to link people to. Everything here is generated from the committed TTL corpus at source/03-standards/ontology/ and guarded by the doc-drift CI gate, so it cannot silently diverge from the model. This page is the entry point; the cards below lead into every layer of the reference.
semanticReframeBlocks.replacementText: This is a draft semantic artefact derived from PDTF 1.0 schemas, dictionaries, documents and recorded decisions. Everything here is generated from the committed TTL corpus at source/03-standards/ontology/ and guarded by the doc-drift CI gate. Reproducible generation makes it a canonical reference for that committed corpus; it does not make the draft an approved standard or the SPDTF 2.0 ontology.
